items.title: JUnit basics
items.context: @Test marks a method as a test case. @BeforeEach/@AfterEach run setup/teardown around every test; @BeforeAll/@AfterAll run once for the whole class. Assertions (assertEquals, assertTrue, ...) check expected outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which annotation marks a method as a JUnit test case?
questions.explanation: @Test is what tells the JUnit runner 'execute this method as a test' — without it, a method is just a plain method.

questions.prompt: Which annotation runs before every single test method in a JUnit 5 test class?
questions.explanation: @BeforeEach runs before each test method (good for resetting fixtures); @BeforeAll runs once for the whole class, typically for expensive shared setup.

items.title: Unit vs integration testing
items.context: A unit test exercises one class/method in isolation, typically mocking its dependencies. An integration test exercises multiple real components together (e.g. a controller through to a real or in-memory database) to verify they work correctly as a group.

questions.prompt: What best distinguishes a unit test from an integration test?
choices: Integration tests never touch a database
A unit test isolates one component (mocking dependencies); an integration test exercises multiple real components together
questions.explanation: Unit tests isolate the thing under test by mocking/stubbing its collaborators; integration tests deliberately wire real components together to catch issues at their boundaries.

items.title: Mockito
items.context: Mockito creates mock objects standing in for real dependencies (@Mock or Mockito.mock()), lets you define their behavior (when(...).thenReturn(...)), and verify interactions afterward (verify(mock).method(...)).

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a Mockito mock object in a unit test?
choices: To stand in for a real dependency so you can isolate and control what it does, without needing the real thing
To replace the need for assertions
To automatically generate test data for a database
To make the test run in a separate thread
questions.explanation: A mock replaces a real collaborator (e.g. a repository or external service) with a controllable fake, so the test only exercises the class under test.

questions.prompt: You want to confirm that a service called `emailSender.send(...)` exactly once during a test. What do you use?
questions.explanation: Mockito's verify(mock, times(n)).method(...) checks how many times a method was actually invoked on a mock — exactly what's needed to assert a side effect happened.

items.title: Testing Spring applications
items.context: @SpringBootTest loads a full (or sliced) Spring ApplicationContext for integration-style tests. Narrower slice annotations (like @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest) load only the relevant part of the context, keeping tests faster.

questions.prompt: Which annotation loads a Spring ApplicationContext for a test, enabling integration-style testing of Spring components together?
questions.explanation: @SpringBootTest bootstraps the application context (fully or via configuration) so the test can exercise real, wired-together Spring beans instead of plain mocks.

items.title: Assertions & test lifecycle
items.context: JUnit assertions (assertEquals, assertTrue, assertThrows, ...) check that actual behavior matches expectations and fail the test with a clear message otherwise. @AfterEach runs cleanup after every test method, mirroring @BeforeEach's setup.

questions.prompt: Which JUnit assertion checks that a boolean condition holds?
questions.explanation: assertTrue(condition) fails the test if the given boolean expression evaluates to false.

questions.prompt: What is @AfterEach typically used for?
choices: Running once before the entire test class
Cleaning up resources after every individual test method
Marking a method as a test case
questions.explanation: @AfterEach runs after each test method, commonly used to release resources or reset state that @BeforeEach set up, keeping tests independent of each other.

items.title: Test doubles: mock, stub & spy
items.context: A mock is a fully fake object with programmed behavior and interaction verification. A spy wraps a real object, letting most calls execute normally while still allowing you to stub or verify specific methods.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between a Mockito @Mock and a @Spy?
choices: @Mock requires a running Spring context, @Spy doesn't
@Mock is entirely fake with no real behavior unless stubbed; @Spy wraps a real object and calls real methods unless specifically stubbed
@Spy can only be used with static methods
questions.explanation: A @Mock has no real implementation behind it — every method returns a default value unless stubbed. A @Spy wraps an actual instance, so unstubbed methods still run their real code.

questions.prompt: You need to test a method on a real object but override just one of its methods to avoid hitting a real external API. What's a good fit?
choices: A @Spy of the real object, with that one method stubbed
Rewriting the class to remove the external call entirely
A plain @Mock of the whole class
questions.explanation: A spy lets the rest of the real object's behavior run normally while you selectively stub out just the one problematic method — exactly the partial-fake use case mocks aren't suited for.

items.title: Parameterized tests
items.context: @ParameterizedTest (JUnit 5) runs the same test method once per supplied input, sourced via @ValueSource, @CsvSource, or a method/enum source — avoiding copy-pasted near-identical test methods for each case.

questions.prompt: Which JUnit 5 annotation runs a single test method repeatedly, once per provided input value?
questions.explanation: @ParameterizedTest, combined with a source annotation like @ValueSource or @CsvSource, executes the same test logic once per supplied argument, avoiding near-duplicate test methods.

items.title: Test-driven development (TDD)
items.context: TDD follows a red-green-refactor cycle: write a failing test for behavior that doesn't exist yet (red), write the minimum code to make it pass (green), then clean up the implementation while keeping tests passing (refactor).

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the classic TDD cycle?
choices: Write a test, delete the code, refactor
Write all the code first, then write tests to match
Refactor, then write code, then write a test
Write a failing test, write code to make it pass, then refactor
questions.explanation: Red-green-refactor: start with a failing test that describes the desired behavior (red), write just enough code to pass it (green), then improve the implementation's design without changing its behavior (refactor).

items.title: Mockito argument matchers
items.context: Argument matchers like any(), anyString(), and eq(value) let you stub or verify a method call without specifying every exact argument — useful when the precise value doesn't matter, or when mixing matchers with exact values.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of Mockito's any() argument matcher?
choices: It asserts the method was never called
It matches any argument of the given type, when the exact value passed doesn't matter for the stub/verification
questions.explanation: any() (and its typed variants like anyString(), anyInt()) let a stub or verify() call match regardless of the specific argument value, useful when only the fact that some call happened matters.

items.title: @MockBean in Spring tests
items.context: @MockBean (Spring Boot Test) replaces a real bean in the test's Spring ApplicationContext with a Mockito mock — useful in @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest slices where you want the rest of the context wired normally but one collaborator (e.g. an external API client) faked.

questions.prompt: What does @MockBean do differently from a plain Mockito @Mock in a Spring test?
choices: @MockBean requires manually registering the bean in XML
@MockBean can only be used outside of Spring
@MockBean replaces the real bean of that type inside the Spring ApplicationContext with a mock, so other beans that depend on it get the mock
questions.explanation: A plain @Mock just creates a standalone mock object; @MockBean additionally injects that mock into the Spring context in place of the real bean, so any other bean wired against that type receives the mock automatically.

items.title: Code coverage & mutation testing
items.context: Code coverage measures what percentage of code was executed while tests ran — a useful signal, but high coverage doesn't guarantee the tests actually check anything meaningful. Mutation testing instead deliberately introduces small bugs ('mutants') into the code and checks whether the test suite catches them, measuring how effective the tests really are.

questions.prompt: What does a code coverage percentage actually tell you?
choices: That the tested code is guaranteed bug-free
What proportion of the code was executed while running the test suite — not whether the assertions are meaningful
How many bugs are currently open
How fast the test suite runs
questions.explanation: Coverage only reports which lines/branches ran during testing; a test can execute a line without ever asserting anything meaningful about its behavior, so 100% coverage is not the same as a thorough test suite.

questions.prompt: What does mutation testing evaluate?
choices: How many classes exist in the codebase
Whether the existing test suite actually detects small deliberately-introduced bugs ('mutants') in the code
The percentage of code that has comments
questions.explanation: Mutation testing tools alter the code in small ways (e.g. flipping a comparison operator) and re-run the tests; a 'mutant' that survives (tests still pass) reveals a gap in what the tests actually verify.

items.title: Arrange-Act-Assert
items.context: The Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern structures a test into three clear parts: set up preconditions and inputs (Arrange), perform the action under test (Act), then verify the outcome (Assert) — making tests easy to read and reason about.

questions.prompt: What does the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern structure within a single test method?
choices: The order test classes run in
Setting up preconditions, performing the action under test, then verifying the result
The naming convention for test methods
questions.explanation: AAA keeps a test's setup, the actual behavior being exercised, and the verification cleanly separated and in a predictable order, making tests much easier to read and maintain.

items.title: Flaky tests
items.context: A flaky test passes and fails intermittently with no code changes — common causes include timing/race conditions, reliance on external services, unordered collections assumed to have an order, or state leaking between tests.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a "flaky" test?
choices: A test that passes and fails intermittently, without any changes to the code under test
A test that runs very slowly
questions.explanation: Flakiness specifically means non-deterministic results — the same test, run against the same code, sometimes passes and sometimes fails — usually pointing to hidden timing dependencies, shared state, or environmental factors.

questions.prompt: A test only fails when run as part of the full suite, never when run alone. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Shared or leaked state between tests — e.g. a static field or a database not properly reset between test runs
Random number generators are banned in tests
questions.explanation: Tests that only fail in combination with others are the classic signature of shared mutable state — a static field, a singleton, or a database/fixture not cleaned up — bleeding over from one test into the next.

items.title: Contract testing
items.context: In a microservices architecture, consumer-driven contract testing verifies that a service's API still satisfies what its consumers actually expect, using lightweight, fast-running contract checks instead of slow, brittle full end-to-end integration tests across every service.

questions.prompt: What does consumer-driven contract testing verify between two services?
choices: That the database schema hasn't changed
That a provider service's API still satisfies the expectations its consumers depend on, without needing full end-to-end tests
questions.explanation: Contract tests capture what each consumer actually expects from a provider's API and check the provider against that contract independently — catching breaking changes early, without the cost and fragility of spinning up every service together for full end-to-end tests.

items.title: Skipping and disabling tests
items.context: @Disabled (JUnit 5) marks a test to be skipped entirely, useful for temporarily excluding a known-broken or not-yet-relevant test without deleting it.

questions.prompt: Which JUnit 5 annotation excludes a test method from being run?
questions.explanation: @Disabled is JUnit 5's annotation for excluding a test (or test class) from execution — JUnit 4 used @Ignore for the equivalent purpose.

items.title: Fakes vs mocks vs stubs
items.context: A stub returns canned answers to calls. A mock additionally lets you verify specific interactions occurred. A fake is a genuinely working, simplified implementation — like an in-memory database standing in for a real one — behaving realistically rather than just returning pre-programmed values.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a "fake" from a mock or stub in testing terminology?
choices: A fake is just another word for mock
A fake is a real, working (but simplified) implementation, like an in-memory database, rather than a pre-programmed stand-in
A fake can only be used in production code
questions.explanation: Mocks and stubs are pre-programmed to return specific canned responses; a fake actually implements real (if simplified) behavior — e.g. an in-memory HashMap-backed 'database' that genuinely stores and retrieves data, just not durably.

items.title: Behavior-driven development (BDD)
items.context: BDD frames test scenarios in a Given-When-Then structure (Given some context, When an action occurs, Then an outcome is expected) — often written in a semi-natural-language format (e.g. with Cucumber) so both technical and non-technical stakeholders can read them.

questions.prompt: Which testing style structures scenarios as Given-When-Then, often in a natural-language format readable by non-developers?
questions.explanation: BDD (via tools like Cucumber) expresses test scenarios as Given/When/Then steps in near-natural language, aiming to be a shared, readable specification for both developers and non-technical stakeholders.

items.title: Spring test slices
items.context: Instead of loading the entire application context with @SpringBootTest for every test, narrower 'slice' annotations load only what's relevant: @WebMvcTest for just the web layer, @DataJpaTest for just the JPA/repository layer, keeping tests focused and fast.

questions.prompt: Which annotation loads only the web/MVC layer (controllers and related infrastructure) for a focused test, rather than the entire application context?
questions.explanation: @WebMvcTest boots up just enough of the Spring context to test controllers (MockMvc, message converters, etc.), skipping the service and repository layers — much faster than a full @SpringBootTest for controller-focused tests.

items.title: Testcontainers
items.context: The Testcontainers library spins up real, disposable Docker containers (a real Postgres, Kafka, Redis, ...) for integration tests, giving far more realistic behavior than mocking or an in-memory substitute, while still being automated and torn down after each test run.

questions.prompt: What does the Testcontainers library provide for integration tests?
choices: A mocking framework for unit tests
Real, disposable Docker containers (e.g. an actual Postgres instance) spun up automatically for integration tests
questions.explanation: Rather than approximating a dependency with an in-memory substitute or mocks, Testcontainers runs the real thing in a throwaway Docker container for the duration of the test suite — much closer to production behavior.

items.title: Fluent assertions with AssertJ
items.context: AssertJ provides fluent, chainable assertions (assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y).isNotNull()) that read more naturally and give richer failure messages than plain JUnit assertions like assertEquals().

questions.prompt: What does a fluent assertion library like AssertJ offer over plain JUnit assertions?
choices: The ability to skip writing assertions entirely
More readable, chainable assertions and typically richer failure messages
questions.explanation: AssertJ's assertThat(...) style lets you chain multiple readable conditions together and generally produces clearer, more descriptive failure output than a sequence of separate assertEquals()/assertTrue() calls.

items.title: The JUnit 5 extension model
items.context: @ExtendWith(SomeExtension.class) registers an extension that hooks into JUnit 5's test lifecycle (before/after each test, parameter resolution, ...) — it replaced JUnit 4's more limited @RunWith, and is how integrations like MockitoExtension or Spring's test support plug in.

questions.prompt: What does @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) on a JUnit 5 test class do?
choices: Registers the Mockito extension, which hooks into the test lifecycle to initialize @Mock-annotated fields automatically
questions.explanation: @ExtendWith plugs a JUnit 5 Extension into the test lifecycle; MockitoExtension specifically initializes fields annotated @Mock/@InjectMocks before each test, replacing the need for manual MockitoAnnotations.openMocks() calls.

items.title: assertThrows for exception testing
items.context: JUnit 5's assertThrows(SomeException.class, () -> { ... }) asserts that running the given block throws exactly that exception type, replacing JUnit 4's older @Test(expected = SomeException.class) attribute — and additionally gives you the thrown exception object to make further assertions on.

questions.prompt: What does assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> doSomething()) verify?
choices: That doSomething() never throws any exception
That doSomething() runs within a time limit
That calling doSomething() throws an IllegalArgumentException, failing the test if it doesn't (or throws something else)
questions.explanation: assertThrows executes the lambda and fails the test unless it throws exactly the specified exception type — and returns that exception instance, letting you assert further on its message or cause.

items.title: ArgumentCaptor
items.context: verify(mock).method(argument) only checks that some value was passed. An ArgumentCaptor lets you actually capture the real argument a mocked method was called with, so you can run further assertions on its contents — useful when you care about the details of what was passed, not just that a call happened.

questions.prompt: What does Mockito's ArgumentCaptor let you do that a plain verify(mock).method(any()) does not?
choices: Capture the actual argument passed to the mocked method call, so you can assert on its specific contents afterward
questions.explanation: ArgumentCaptor.capture() grabs the real object passed into a mocked call during verify(), letting you inspect its fields/state directly — going beyond just confirming that some call with some argument happened.

items.title: Mockito verify call-count variants
items.context: Beyond times(n), Mockito offers never() (equivalent to times(0)), atLeastOnce(), atLeast(n), and atMost(n) as more expressive alternatives for asserting how often a mocked method was invoked.

questions.prompt: Which Mockito verification mode asserts that a mocked method was never called?
questions.explanation: verify(mock, never()).someMethod() is the idiomatic way to assert a method was not invoked at all — equivalent to, but more readable than, times(0).

items.title: @Nested test classes
items.context: JUnit 5's @Nested lets you group related test methods into inner classes within a test class, each able to have its own @BeforeEach setup — improving organization and making shared context between related scenarios explicit.

questions.prompt: What does JUnit 5's @Nested annotation enable?
choices: Grouping related tests into inner classes within a test class, each with their own lifecycle callbacks
Running tests in a separate JVM process
questions.explanation: @Nested marks an inner class as containing its own group of tests, letting you organize scenarios hierarchically (e.g. "when the cart is empty" / "when the cart has items") with shared or scenario-specific setup, instead of one flat list of test methods.

items.title: Injecting a Clock for time-dependent tests
items.context: Code that calls Instant.now()/LocalDate.now() directly is hard to test deterministically, since the actual result depends on the moment the test happens to run. Injecting a java.time.Clock (defaulting to Clock.systemDefaultZone() in production) lets a test supply a fixed clock instead, making time-dependent behavior fully reproducible.

questions.prompt: A service computes whether a subscription has expired by calling LocalDate.now() directly, making the logic hard to test reliably. What's a common fix?
choices: Mock the JVM's system clock globally
Inject a java.time.Clock into the service (real Clock in production, a fixed one in tests) instead of calling now() directly
questions.explanation: By depending on an injected Clock rather than calling static now() methods, tests can supply Clock.fixed(...) to pin 'the current time' to any exact instant, making expiry logic and similar time-dependent behavior deterministic and easy to test at boundary conditions.

items.title: Strict vs lenient stubbing
items.context: Modern Mockito defaults to strict stubbing: if a test sets up a stub (when(...).thenReturn(...)) that the code under test never actually calls, Mockito flags it as a likely mistake (UnnecessaryStubbingException) rather than silently ignoring it. lenient() opts a specific stub out of that check when the unused stub is intentional.

questions.prompt: What does Mockito's strict stubbing do with a stub that the test never actually exercises?
choices: It causes all other stubs in the test to fail too
Nothing — unused stubs are always silently ignored
It flags the unused stub as a likely mistake (e.g. via UnnecessaryStubbingException), unless it's explicitly marked lenient()
It automatically removes the stub from the test file
questions.explanation: Strict stubbing treats a configured-but-never-called stub as a signal something's off (often a sign the test is checking the wrong thing, or a leftover from a refactor) — lenient() is the explicit escape hatch for the rare case where that's actually intentional.

items.title: Test lifecycle ordering
items.context: For a JUnit 5 test class: any @BeforeAll method runs once, before anything else. Then, for each test method: @BeforeEach runs, then the @Test method, then @AfterEach — and finally @AfterAll runs once after every test in the class has finished.

questions.prompt: In what order do @BeforeAll and @BeforeEach run relative to each other?
choices: @BeforeAll runs once before any tests; @BeforeEach then runs before every individual test method
They run in a random order
questions.explanation: @BeforeAll (a static, once-per-class hook) runs a single time before any test in the class starts; @BeforeEach then runs fresh before every single @Test method, resetting whatever per-test state is needed.

items.title: @TestPropertySource
items.context: @TestPropertySource lets a Spring test override or supply specific properties just for that test class's context — handy for testing behavior under different configuration values without maintaining a whole separate profile-specific properties file.

questions.prompt: What does @TestPropertySource(properties = "feature.x.enabled=true") do on a Spring test class?
choices: Requires a separate Spring profile to work
Overrides that specific property for the test's Spring context only, without touching the real configuration file
questions.explanation: @TestPropertySource injects or overrides properties scoped to that test class's ApplicationContext, letting you exercise a specific configuration value in isolation without maintaining a dedicated properties file for it.

items.title: Mocking static methods
items.context: Classic Mockito mocks work by subclassing or proxying an instance, which doesn't apply to static methods. Mockito's mockStatic() (backed by mockito-inline) specifically supports stubbing static methods within a try-with-resources block — though relying on it heavily is often a sign the code should be refactored toward more testable, non-static dependencies.

questions.prompt: Can classic Mockito mocking (@Mock, Mockito.mock()) intercept calls to a static method?
choices: Static methods can never be tested at all
No — static methods require Mockito's separate mockStatic() support (via mockito-inline), since classic mocking works by subclassing/proxying instances
Only final classes support static mocking
questions.explanation: Regular Mockito mocks are built by creating a proxy subclass of the target type, which has no bearing on static method calls; mockStatic() is a distinct, more invasive mechanism specifically for intercepting static calls, and heavy reliance on it often signals code that would benefit from being restructured for easier testing.

items.title: Calling an unstubbed mock method (primitive return)

questions.prompt: What does this print, given add() was never stubbed?
choices: 0 — Mockito returns a sensible default value for the method's return type
Throws NullPointerException — unstubbed calls aren't allowed
questions.explanation: By default (non-strict, unstubbed) Mockito mocks don't throw for un-stubbed calls — they return a type-appropriate default: 0 for int/long, false for boolean, and null for object return types. This surprises people expecting either the real logic or an exception; it's neither.

items.title: Calling an unstubbed mock method (object return)

questions.prompt: What does this print, given findName() was never stubbed?
questions.explanation: For an unstubbed method returning an object type, Mockito's default answer is null, not an empty value or an exception — contrast this with a primitive return type, which gets 0/false instead, since null isn't a valid primitive value. This distinction quietly causes NullPointerExceptions later in test code that assumes a stub was set up.

items.title: @Mock field left null without MockitoExtension

questions.prompt: What happens when this test runs?
choices: repo is null, so when(repo.find(1))... throws NullPointerException
Mockito silently creates a real Repo instance instead
questions.explanation: The @Mock annotation only declares intent — something has to actually process it and inject the mock, either @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) on the test class or an explicit MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in a @BeforeEach. Without either, repo is never initialized and stays null, so calling repo.find(1) throws a plain NullPointerException, not a Mockito-specific error.

items.title: verify() with the wrong invocation count

questions.prompt: What happens when this verify() call runs?
choices: Fails, throwing a Mockito verification error reporting 1 actual invocation vs 2 wanted
Passes — times() only checks a minimum
questions.explanation: verify(mock, times(n)) asserts an exact invocation count. Since save() was actually called once but the test demands exactly two, Mockito fails the test with a verification exception (something like "Wanted 2 times but was 1 time") — times() is exact, not a floor; use atLeast()/atMost() for open-ended counts.

items.title: UnnecessaryStubbingException for an unused stub

questions.prompt: What happens when this test runs?
choices: Fails at the end of the test with UnnecessaryStubbingException
Fails immediately at the when(...) line
Passes normally — unused stubs are just ignored
Only prints a warning to the console, test still passes
questions.explanation: Since Mockito 2's strict stubbing (default when using MockitoExtension/MockitoJUnitRunner), a stub that's set up but never actually exercised by the code under test is flagged as likely dead/wrong test setup. Mockito reports it as an UnnecessaryStubbingException at the end of the test run, specifically to catch stale stubs left over from refactoring.

items.title: PotentialStubbingProblem: stubbed vs actual arguments

questions.prompt: What happens on this call, under Mockito's default strict stubbing?
choices: Throws PotentialStubbingProblem, since 1 was stubbed but a different argument (2) was used
questions.explanation: PotentialStubbingProblem is Mockito's way of flagging "you stubbed this method, but with different arguments than what's actually being called" — a strong signal that either the test setup or the code under test has a bug (e.g. an off-by-one in which id gets passed). It's a different failure than UnnecessaryStubbingException (a stub never invoked at all with any arguments).

items.title: assertThrows() when the code doesn't throw

questions.prompt: What happens when this test runs?
choices: Passes, because assertThrows() only checks IF an exception is thrown, not that one must be
Fails — assertThrows() itself throws an AssertionError because the expected exception never occurred
questions.explanation: assertThrows(type, executable) requires the given code to throw an exception of that type — if it completes normally instead, assertThrows() itself fails the test with an AssertionError ("Expected IllegalArgumentException to be thrown, but nothing was thrown"). It's not just a passive check; a lack of an exception is itself a test failure here.

items.title: Mocking a final method without mockito-inline

questions.prompt: What happens, using classic (non-inline) Mockito without the mockito-inline extension?
choices: The classic Mockito mock maker (subclassing) can't override a final method, so stubbing it has no effect (or mocking fails outright, depending on version)
Works exactly like mocking any other method
Throws UnsupportedOperationException at the when() call specifically
questions.explanation: Classic Mockito creates mocks by generating a subclass and overriding methods — but Java doesn't allow overriding a final method at all, so that mechanism simply can't intercept calls to find(). Depending on the Mockito/JVM version this either silently falls through to real behavior or fails to create the mock in the first place; the mockito-inline (or Mockito 5's default inline mock maker) uses bytecode instrumentation instead, which can handle final classes/methods.

items.title: What ArgumentCaptor actually captures

questions.prompt: What does captor.getValue() give you?
choices: The literal string "hello" passed into service.process()
Throws an exception if save() was called more than zero times
The actual argument that was passed to mock.save(...) inside service.process(), whatever the code transformed it into
null, since captors only work with verify(mock, times(1))
questions.explanation: ArgumentCaptor doesn't capture what you passed to the method under test — it captures what your code under test passed to the *mock*. Combined with verify(), it lets you assert on the actual (possibly transformed/derived) value the code produced internally, which plain equality stubbing can't easily inspect.

items.title: @InjectMocks leaving an unmocked dependency null

questions.prompt: What happens when service.charge() runs in this test?
choices: Mockito creates a real Logger instance to fill the gap
@InjectMocks throws an exception at test startup because not all constructor args have mocks
logger stays null (no @Mock for it was declared), so logger.log(...) throws NullPointerException
Both gateway and logger are mocked automatically
questions.explanation: @InjectMocks only fills in constructor/field slots for which a matching @Mock (or @Spy) exists in the test class — it does not fail loudly if one is missing, it just leaves that field null (or unset) and proceeds. Here, since no @Mock Logger was declared, logger stays null inside the constructed PaymentService, and the first real use of it — logger.log(...) — throws a plain NullPointerException at runtime, often confusingly far from the actual root cause.
